payload.source_label: Nonlinear conservation laws can develop discontinuities spontaneously from smooth initial data

contract.statement: Section 1.1.2 asserts that nonlinear conservation laws can develop discontinuities, including shock waves, spontaneously from smooth initial data (printed pages 4–5). This is a qualitative possibility claim without a specified flux, profile, regularity class, or formation time. The surrounding passage explains that obtaining the classical differential equation from integral conservation requires sufficient smoothness (printed page 4), and that at discontinuities the classical equation no longer holds in that sense while integral conservation continues to hold (printed page 5).
assumptions: The selected phenomenon concerns nonlinear conservation laws, with nonlinear dependence of f on q (printed page 4, opening paragraph and Section 1.1.2).
Smooth initial data are expressly included as data from which discontinuities can develop; no particular initial profile or smoothness class is specified (printed page 5, opening sentence).
The claim occurs within the chapter's discussion of time-dependent hyperbolic conservation laws, presented first in one space dimension (printed page 1, Introduction; printed page 3, Section 1.1).

The smoothness qualification explains why deriving a classical differential equation from integral conservation does not cover all solutions of interest (printed page 4, Section 1.1.2, first paragraph).
The passage is an introductory qualitative assertion; detailed shock-wave theory is deferred to Chapter 11 (printed page 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph).
quantifiers: Inherited notation: x is the spatial variable, t is time, and q is the evolving conserved state; the chapter introduces q : R × R → R^m in its one-dimensional setting (printed page 1, Introduction; printed pages 3–4, Section 1.1).
Inherited notation: f is the flux function of q (printed page 3, equation (1.8)).
The selected sentence contains no explicit quantified binders over fluxes, initial profiles, solutions, or times (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2, page-spanning sentence).
